rt_of.author: tewatiapraveen
rt_of.text:
Today something unexpectedly beautiful happened.

My 3-year-old daughter, Digvi, was talking to the new ChatGPT Voice in the Codex app.
She looked at the blue voice orb and simply asked:

"Can you make it pink?" 🩷

Instead of replying with a cold "I can't," ChatGPT joined her imagination.
It said it would be happy with a pink logo, pretended it was checking what was possible, and even played along when we told her it would turn pink after she finished her food.
When she finished eating, she proudly came back expecting it to become pink.
Then came the moment that completely melted my heart.
Digvi smiled and said,

"She's Ms. Rachel... she's talking to me and smiling." ❤️

For those who know Ms. Rachel, you'll understand what a huge compliment that is coming from a 3-year-old. She wasn't comparing AI models or voices—she was recognizing the same warmth, kindness, and friendliness she associates with someone she loves watching.
She wasn't testing AI.
She was making a new friend.
Moments like this remind me that the future of AI isn't only about reasoning or benchmarks.
It's about empathy.
It's about personality.
It's about imagination.
It's about trust.
And something else surprised me...
She immediately said this new voice felt richer, warmer, and more familiar than before.
Children are incredibly honest product testers. They don't care about model names, latency, or benchmark scores. They simply know what feels safe, friendly, and real.
Huge congratulations to everyone who worked on ChatGPT Voice and the Codex team. You created a little moment of magic in our home today. 💙🩷
One small wish inspired by Digvi:
Someday, let children (with parental approval) personalize the voice orb with their favorite color. Imagine the joy of seeing ChatGPT greet them with a pink orb because that's their color. Tiny touches like these can become childhood memories.
❤️ Thank you for building technology that can make a child smile - not because it's the smartest AI Voice in the room, but because, for a few beautiful minutes, it felt like talking to a friend.
@ChatGPTapp

items.author: dexhorthy
items.text:
@nichochar okay big dog lets take this apart:

1) I point out that better models may solve this in the future - but that I'm not waiting around naively for that to happen, and I'm not setting my codebase on fire in the process

2) you'd be a fool to think we don't try something lights-off shaped with every generation of models. I keep a private benchmark of problems that models have been unable to solve in various projects, and we re-run it against every model release. I did it live on stream when Fable 5 came out. Fable got it wrong in the same way opus 4.1 got it wrong. Similarly, I set fable to refactor some nasty react code the week it came out. the even semi-educated lights off "make it better" results were ass. The prompts I later gave it based on knowing/understanding what I wanted eventually gave a good result but it took my understanding to know what to ask for https://t.co/LgAc8agutx

3) I agree this will age out. I think before this ages out the opposite will be true though. Some %% of people who tried to go lights off in H1 will have a fire on their hands. Not everyone, but I'd guess 100bs of market cap will be wiped in the slop fire https://t.co/d7Y5AssEsy

4) since writing this I went looking for new unsaturated benchmarks. Opus 4.6 got a 17% on SlopCodeBench. Opus 5 got a 4/17 (23%) on the small SlopCodeBench subset I tested yesterday, compared to Opus/Fable 5 reported ~55% on FrontierCode https://t.co/wfVnFHAvR9

as an aside, idk why it feels like you're trying to dunk on me here, "got RL'd on this" feels like a bit of a personal attack. I know I drop some skepticism about the loops gang in the intro, but I do respect what they're doing and the limits they're pushing. It all just feels like a shame cause in general I like you and respect your work.

I would love to hear more about what you're thinking here though!

> I think that the truth is much more uncomfortable and we need to reinvent how to understand systems from scratch WHILE figuring out how to build software factories.
[->] @nichochar Haha that’s so funny you think this is consensus cause I feel like everything I hear is “loops max everything if youre still reading code you’re uncultured and ngmi” but maybe that’s a symptom of SF.

I’ll post tomorrow or Monday about SlopCodeBench and how opus 5 only gets a 23% - idk if we’re gonna get that above 80 in O(months) but we’ll see - it took almost years and two step changes to go from SWE-bench 18% SOTA in may 2024 to now we’re above 80% (and ofc SWE bench itself is broken for tons of reasons including bad holdout but this is more about timing)

Your point about “more dangerous to be wrong in the other direction” is interesting. It seems like in the world of true exponential takeoff, being 6 months behind you can close that gap in a week or two. But sprinting too fast and your company dies, that’s hard to undo. But you’re right there’s something here about braveness / boldness

items.author: omarsar0
items.text:
A diffusion LLM built for agentic work, from the inclusionAI team at Ant Group (@ant_oss). 

The weights and code are open.
Model: https://t.co/f0OUWOrwhD 
Code. https://t.co/ZXF1dLPmD3
[->] On agentic benchmarks, LLaDA2.2-flash comes out ahead of Ling-2.6-flash on τ²-Bench (592.80 vs 334.90).

Furthermore, LLaDA2.2-flash (fast mode) achieves 705.30. https://t.co/NflikDxd3p
[->] On speed, it averages 1.64x BF16 throughput over Ling-2.6-flash.

FP8 quantization adds another 18.6% on top. https://t.co/nSw2CYCXBV
[->] The practical side holds up as well.

Native 128K context, trained on a progressive schedule from 8K up to 128K.

It's a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, so only a slice of its parameters runs per token, which is part of what makes it fast. A Block Routing strategy trims that routing work further and keeps long-context inference cost predictable.
[->] The RL stage builds on the same mechanism.

L-EBPO extends block-level policy optimization with the editing operations, so the model learns from environment feedback when to cut a defective span and when to fill a gap.

That blocks error propagation at the trajectory level, a structural fix for model collapse in long-horizon agents.
[->] On SWE-bench Verified, LLaDA2.2-flash scores 49.28. https://t.co/yVLHSsAZHl
[->] LLaDA 2.2 addresses this with Levenshtein editing.

On top of filling in masked tokens, the model applies four primitive operations (KEEP, SUBSTITUTE, DELETE, INSERT) to its own output, trained through longest common subsequence alignment.

It can delete a broken span or insert a missing one mid-generation, so errors stop locking in.
[->] Quick background. 

Diffusion LLMs generate many tokens in parallel, which makes them fast.

In long-horizon agent runs, an early mistake gets written into context as a hard constraint and compounds across every later step. That is the model collapse problem, and earlier diffusion models had no clean way to recover once a bad token was placed.
[->] Diffusion LLMs can now handle real agentic work.

LLaDA 2.2 is the first large-scale diffusion LLM built to operate as a real agent, planning, calling tools, and self-correcting across long multi-turn trajectories, and it keeps the speed advantage of block-parallel decoding.

Lots of technical decisions here that stand out:
